near_miss.lead: ON hlýða/lýðr ~ ORu. слышаша людье 'the people heard'
near_miss.why_not: hlýða and слышати are both from *ḱlew- but differently formed; 'the people heard' is ordinary narrative language, and lýða in the pivot is a scribal doublet of hlýða, not 'people'.
the partners have no gesture of supplication; falling at someone's feet is a general gesture with no cognate wording.

near_miss.lead: ON legal pair líf ok limar / lífs grið ok lima 'life and limbs'
near_miss.why_not: alliterative pair from Norse law, known only in Germanic (cf. Engl. life and limb); no partner has 'life + limb'. Gk ὠλένας (Ion 1403) is not cognate with limr (ὠλένη ~ ON ǫln). I know no comparandum outside Germanic.

near_miss.lead: ON bjóða fé fyrir mann ~ Ved. paśūn (*péḱu) with men/progeny
near_miss.why_not: fé here means money/wergild, not part of a 'men and cattle' list; the AV line is a wish for progeny, sight and cattle. Shared root, no shared collocation.

near_miss.lead: ON þjóð galt (the people paid) / ríg na túath (king of the peoples), with *tewteh2- on both sides
near_miss.why_not: *tewteh2- is cognate but the collocations differ: ON 'the people paid for the ruler's wrath' vs. MIr. 'king of the peoples'. The pivot's ræsir is not *h3reǵ-, and fogelmais is too uncertain to set beside gjalda.

near_miss.lead: type scene: others slept but one lay awake (ON konungrinn vakti en aðrir menn sváfu ~ Il. 24.677-9 εὗδον ... ἀλλ' οὐχ Ἑρμείαν ... ὕπνος ἔμαρπτεν)
near_miss.why_not: congruent scene, but the only cognate is *swep- (ON verb sofa vs. Gk noun ὕπνος) and the device is a narrative commonplace found everywhere; nothing makes it diagnostic.

near_miss.lead: þegja ~ tacēre + orð ~ uerbum 'silent, (did) not (say) a word'; also silence beside joy (þagði ... kátr ok glaðr ~ tacitus taceas ... gaudeas)
near_miss.why_not: the lexical match is an exclusive Germanic–Italic isogloss, but 'be silent, say not a word' is the obvious way to put it. The search found the ON idiom þegir ok mælir ekki orð 9 times and Latin only once (PlCurcu 21). kátr ~ gaudeo is etymologically doubtful.

near_miss.lead: kinship statement 'his mother is the sister of X' (ON móðir mín er systir hans ~ Arm. մաւր ... քոյր արքային ~ OIr. siair a máthar), with a sister's son as the central link
near_miss.why_not: exact cognates (*méh2tēr, *swésōr) in a congruent avunculate context, but any IE language states this relation with its inherited kin terms; it is description, not phraseology.

near_miss.lead: ON binda sætt ok frið 'bind peace'
near_miss.why_not: Skt bandhu (kinsman) only shares the root; 'bind a truce' is common legal metaphor, and no partner binds peace or a treaty.

near_miss.lead: giving a king's daughter in marriage (ON konungs dóttir ... gipt ~ Arm. տալ ... զդուստր իմ ի կնութիւն)
near_miss.why_not: *dʰugh2tḗr is cognate and the verbs are renewed (gipta vs. tam), but giving a daughter in marriage is universal content with no fixed wording.

near_miss.lead: merism nótt ok dag (night first) ~ Gk νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ
near_miss.why_not: the slab partners hold only νυκτός/νύξ, not the merism. ON has both orders (dag ok nótt in AM-36-fol 142 w32), and 'night and day' is generic everywhere.

near_miss.lead: sunrise phrasing: rann upp sól / sólin svá há ~ sol ... obire / udite sūrye
near_miss.why_not: the only cognate is *sóh2wl̥; the verbs differ (renna vs. obire/ud-i), and the sun rising is generic.

near_miss.lead: hallæri vs ár mikit (bad vs good season) ~ ὥρα
near_miss.why_not: *yeh1r- is on both sides, but the Greek is about weather outside the season and food shortage in a campaign, not the Norse ár 'harvest plenty' concept; no shared collocation.
